title: Do tabloids poison the well of social media? Explaining democratically dysfunctional news sharing
screen_reason: Custom survey of 1,313 UK Twitter users during the 2017 UK general election reports self-reported shares of respondents who shared inaccurate, exaggerated or made-up news on social media in the past month (Table 3): 67.7% any, 29.9% unwittingly shared made-up news, 17.1% knowingly exaggerated, 8.9% knowingly made-up. These are RECALL sharing shares with a population denominator.

estimates.date: survey fielded 5-11 June 2017 (2017 UK general election campaign)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who recall sharing news on social media in the past month that was inaccurate, exaggerated or made up (any of four options)
estimates.value_raw: 67.7% (complement of the 391/1210, 32.3% who selected no response option)
estimates.denominator: 1,210 UK Twitter users answering the dysfunctional-news-sharing item (from 1,313 surveyed respondents recruited from Twitter users who shared or followed UK tabloids)
estimates.definition: Respondent selected at least one of: shared news that seemed accurate but was later found made up; was exaggerated and they were unaware; was exaggerated and they were aware; they thought was made up when they shared it
estimates.misinfo_def: Sometimes people might share news on social media that turns out not to be fully accurate or is exaggerated
estimates.source_quote: Fully two-thirds (67.7%) admitted to having shared news that was problematic in some way in the past month.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-report on a four-option checklist adapted from the Pew Research Center 2016 fake-news report; no external verification
estimates.moderator_quote: Users were invited to take our survey from 5 June to 8 June 2017 and we kept it open until 11 June, 3 days after Election Day. In total, 1422 users completed our survey—a participation rate of 3.6%
estimates.notes: Broadest definition row. The 67.7% is stated verbatim in the text; it corresponds to the 100 - 32.3% of Table 3 who selected no option, but the value itself is printed by the authors, so R8 is satisfied. Denominator is the Table 3 total (1,210), not the 1,313 analysed respondents, because 103 did not answer the item.

estimates.date: survey fielded 5-11 June 2017 (2017 UK general election campaign)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who recall knowingly sharing news on social media in the past month that they thought was made up
estimates.value_raw: 4. You thought was made up when you shared it 108 8.9
estimates.denominator: 1,210 UK Twitter users answering the dysfunctional-news-sharing item
estimates.definition: Respondent selected 'You thought was made up when you shared it' (the paper's disinformation category)
estimates.misinfo_def: Sometimes people might share news on social media that turns out not to be fully accurate or is exaggerated
estimates.source_quote: In particular, 8.9% admitted to having willfully shared news that was made up and 17.1% willfully shared news that was exaggerated.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-report on a four-option checklist adapted from the Pew Research Center 2016 fake-news report; no external verification
estimates.moderator_quote: "You thought was made up when you shared it" (scored 4)
estimates.notes: Strictest definition variant of the same item: knowing (willful) sharing of fabricated news.

estimates.moderator_quote: We rank-ordered the different behaviors to build a scale ranging from no reported dysfunctional news sharing (0), through misinformation to the most egregious offense of disinformation (4).
estimates.notes: Unwitting-sharing definition variant. Table cell copied verbatim, including the column spacing; the row label continues on the next line as 'was made up'. Options were not mutually exclusive (respondents could select more than one), so these categories cannot be summed. The table row number ('1.') is dropped from the quoted span because the extracted text carries a control character between it and the label.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) 17.1% who knowingly shared exaggerated news and 31.3% who unknowingly shared exaggerated news — same item, further definition variants; kept out to avoid stacking near-duplicate rows on one survey question (R4), and they cannot be summed with the rows above because respondents could choose more than one option; (b) 35.1% who reported being challenged on social media for sharing news that was not fully accurate, and the components (18.4% not fully accurate, 8.9% exaggerated, 7.8% completely made up) — this measures receiving a correction, not sharing or being exposed to misinformation, so it is not one of the review's constructs; (c) 'just 329 domains accounted for 90% of all the domains our users shared' — a concentration statistic about all shared news domains, not about misinformation, so it does not qualify as a CONCENTRATION row under R1; (d) 21% shared one or no tabloid stories, 13% shared one or more per day — tabloid sharing, not misinformation; (e) the model-predicted probabilities (62%, 72%, 52%, 43%, 39%, 23%) are regression predictions for hypothetical average respondents, not observed shares.

rob.design: Hybrid design: a custom survey of Twitter users invited by automated @message from a defined population of 39,639 users who had shared a UK tabloid political article (15-22 May 2017) or followed a tabloid account, filtered for bots and organisational accounts; 1,422 completed (3.6% participation rate), 1,313 retained after an attention check; linked to 1,525,748 collected tweets from 1,289 respondents. Outcome measures are self-report checklists; no coder reliability applies. The sample is not representative of the UK population and the authors say so.
